utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please could you call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Tecla Benjamin, Ekkehard Withopf, and the case manager, Kimberly Fleming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Appearances for the Defence. It seems that somebody is lacking amongst you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr. President. Edina Residovic and Alexis Demirdjian, legal assistant. Mr. Stephane Bourgon, my co-counsel, has a previous commitment and he's going to join us during the first break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The other Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, Rodney Dixon, and Mr. Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber greets everybody present in the courtroom, the representatives of the OTP, of the Defence, the accused, as well as everybody else present in the courtroom, and in particular the interpreters, who are doing an excellent job and who help the Chamber in their work. Today on our schedule we have two witnesses; one who is coming for the cross-examination, and then the second witness. But before begin the cross-examination, I'm going to ask Mr. Registrar to move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. You have returned to us. Yesterday you were examined by the Prosecution. Within this procedure, the Defence of the accused are also going to put some questions to you. As I already told you yesterday, when giving your answers, take your time; answer as completely as possible. If you don't understand the question, ask the person who has put it to you to rephrase it. And as I've already told you, the Judges also may ask you questions, and after that the Prosecution will have the right to re-examine you, should they wish to do so. I don't want to take any more of your time. I would like to enable you to go home as soon as possible. I am giving the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Marjanovic. My name is Edina Residovic. I am Defence counsel for General Hadzihasanovic. I will ask you to answer some of my questions. Is it true that before today's testimony you gave a statement about the events at several places immediately after you were rescued at the police station. Then also, two or three days after you managed to save yourself you gave a statement to some foreigners who visited you; and you also gave an interview for television and newspapers? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So what -- you're saying that you never before gave a statement about this event.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did give a statement about the event that I spoke about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. So two or three days after you managed to save yourself from being shot, you spoke about the event in the way it really happened; is that true?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then your memory was much more complete and better than ten years later.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. It should be the case. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to some questions that my learned friend asked you. You said that you were born and raised in Paklarevo village, which is between Turbe and Travnik in Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that true?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your village is at the foot of Mount Vlasic; is that true?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were a farmer, that you were engaged in cattle raising, and the area where you reside is very well known for cattle raising; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In March 1992, you noticed that the Serbs in the vicinity of your village and in the general area of Travnik started digging trenches, and especially on Mount Galica, which is part of Mount Vlasic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A month later, sometime in April 1992, the first shell from the Serb positions from Mount Vlasic started falling on your village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After that day, you could also hear sniper fire in your village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that was the reason for which you, as you told us yesterday, able-bodied men in the village, decided to organise yourselves and set up guards in order to protect your village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we organised ourselves, and we guard our village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You participated in village guards and you had a pistol; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of May, a shell fell on the village and it injured you severely; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You sustained severe injuries at that time. A shrapnel of the shell which had been fired from the Serb positions hit you in the head; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The shell was fired, and I was wounded by the shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And although you were taken to the hospital in Travnik, the doctors there could not remove the shrapnel because of the complications.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not just one shrapnel that wasn't removed. I had several shrapnels -- I have several shrapnels in my body that haven't been removed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that after a certain period of treatment which lasted for 10 or 15 days, you didn't return to your village, Paklarevo, but to Maljine, where the situation was somewhat more peaceful; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In Maljine village, there was mixed population, both Muslim and Croat.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they were separated. The Croats were higher up and Muslims were lower down.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when you arrived there and a few months after that, there were no conflicts in the village between the Muslims and the Croats. On the contrary, they guarded the lines facing the Serbian positions in the direction of Vlasic together; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the vicinity of Maljine, there is the village of Mehurici, where the inhabitants are mostly Muslims; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While you were staying in Maljine, you occasionally went to Mehurici, and on a market day you were able to see some foreigners there who looked different from the local inhabitants; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, they had taken over some Serbian houses in the village of Poljanice, in the immediate vicinity of Mehurici; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they took over -- occupied some houses, but I saw them down in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you were able to notice that some of the local Muslims occasionally started joining these foreigners and imitating them; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the spring of 1993, as you were on sick leave and were able to follow the news on the radio and the television, you noticed that the general situation as far as the army and HVO relationship was concerned had deteriorated.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about Vitez that in -- and I heard about Busovaca and Novi Travnik. I heard about that on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Such news also had an effect on the fear felt by the local population; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In March 1993, the Frankopan Brigade was founded. Its headquarters were in the monastery in Guca Gora, and most of the men who were fit from military service from Maljine were part of that brigade; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be quite frank, I don't know what the name of the brigade was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you do know that the men who were fit for military service from Maljine were HVO members.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were HVO members, but I don't know what the name of the brigade was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You did not join that brigade because of your injuries; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, HVO members from the village started establishing certain defence lines facing the BH army; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they would dig in in their direction, which is what the BH army did too with regard to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As of that date, the HVO members from Maljine no longer went to the lines in Vlasic but they stayed at the positions around the village; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of June, 1993 you said that you were at home with your family; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you heard shooting, you went down to the basement with your wife and your children.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You heard that they were firing from the hill, but as you were in the basement, you were not able to see the soldiers or the insignia they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in the basement all the time. I put my family in the basement. But occasionally I would have a look outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You heard that for some time the HVO returned fire from positions around the village, but this soon ceased and you came to the conclusion that those positions had fallen.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was returning fire. I just heard intense shooting. But as to who was doing the shooting, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After some time, you were asked to surrender. And after negotiations held in the village, you yourself surrendered.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of those negotiations with army representatives, a doctor from the village participated in these negotiations; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You then handed over your pistol, which you had taken with you from Paklarevo after you had been wounded and after you had arrived in Maljine; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hand it over.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Because of the overall situation, and in particular because of the fact that you were with your children, you were afraid and you didn't pay any attention to the insignia that the army members were wearing.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The BH army members did have insignia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You headed towards Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And on the way there, you were escorted by BH army soldiers; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During the entire trip, you were treated fairly.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, up until Bikosi Gora. Then we were shoved into some sort of a car.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true to say that when you had passed through the village of Poljanice, four or five men, three Mujahedin, and two Muslims met you? They had green masks over their faces, and they were taking 15 Croats with them from the first group that had left Maljine.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Because of the masks that these persons were wearing, you couldn't recognise the local Muslims.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You only noticed that one of the local Muslims was acting as an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not just one of them; there were -- yes, he was acting as an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you said that you were at the back of the column and at the time you were carrying your small child, you didn't even pay attention and you didn't hear what the Mujahedin told the soldiers who were escorting you.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the back of the column, they separated me with that group.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but before, when they had only just arrived, at the beginning of the column. You don't know whether they spoke to the soldiers who were escorting you.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they did speak about something, but I don't know what the subject was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said that they separated you. You handed over your underaged child to your wife. And they then took you towards Bikosi; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These Mujahedin and the local Muslims who were masked escorted you as far as Bikosi in fact; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I won't go over everything that you said, but is it true that they shot at you in Bikosi when Mijo Tavic, who was in your group, started screaming because he had an epileptic fit?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after that scream, you could hear shooting.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You fell to the ground, and you remained on the ground until the situation calmed down. After that, according to what you said, you and several others who had survived managed to escape and to reach the village of Sarici, after which the HVO took you to Nova Bila; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. Marjanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Is there any cross-examination for the other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we don't have any questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, before the Prosecution takes the floor, there is just one matter I would like to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thanks to the cross-examination, we have discovered that in fact you were the victim of three shots in 1992, before June, and at least two of the shots came from the Serbs. And you said, in response to a question, that you still have pieces of shrapnel in your body that resulted from the shots fired by the Serbs. Is that what you have testified? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the pieces of shrapnel are the result of the grenades thrown by the Serbs. And the wound I have below my left knee, that is what happened when I was shot at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So yesterday I asked you a question about the nature of the bullet that hit you below the left knee. According to what you have told us - and this is also what came out in the course of the cross-examination - we have discovered that when someone had an epileptic fit there was an incident. A shot was fired. As far as you can remember, this was the 8th of June, 1993, so it happened a long time ago. But such events do remain in one's memory. The shots fired, were they rifle shots or was it a burst of fire from a machine-gun? Were these individual shots, or were they bursts of fire? Do you remember anything about this?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, there was a burst of fire. And after the burst of fire, individual shots were fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And when you were wounded, was this the result of a burst of fire or of an individual shot?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a burst of fire that hit me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you said that you were wounded as a result of a burst of fire. So it must have been from a machine-gun, rather than a rifle. What conclusion would you draw from this fact?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were automatic rifles which fired bursts of fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The wound that you sustained in your left leg, in your opinion was it a serious wound, a superficial wound, very -- a very serious wound, an average wound? How would you describe it? Because it was an entry and exit wound, as far as we have understood; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It passed through the area below my left knee, but it wasn't a serious wound. If the wound had been serious, I wouldn't have been able to escape from that place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you are telling us that the wound wasn't very serious.

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it wasn't very serious. If it had been a serious wound, I wouldn't have been able to escape from that site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when you escaped, did you have to limp or were you able to walk without great problems?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had certain difficulties, but I was able to run without it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you escaped after those who had fired had left. Or did you escape -- or were you escaping at the same time that the shooting was ongoing?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they dispersed, that is when I escaped. I wouldn't have been able to escape if they had been present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you waited for them to leave. And when they left, how many of them were there? You were present. Were you able to count them? How many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were about seven or eight of them, because a small group led us from down there. And when we went closer to Bikosi, others joined them. But there were about seven or eight of them in the group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And before they left, they didn't try to check the number of dead or wounded?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before they left, they fired individual shots. I think they were alternate shots, because otherwise I wouldn't have got away, because they shot some of them in the head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you're saying that they shot at random at those who were on the ground before they left, and you were fortunate and weren't hit. Is that how we are to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BERISLAV MARJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't hit me. They probably shot at those who were moving a lot. They wanted to help them die quickly, probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for these clarifications concerning the character of your wound, because in the indictment it is stated that you sustained a serious wound. But from a medical point of view it's very difficult to assess the nature of your wound, because we don't have any documents apart from your statement. I'm going to address the Prosecution now to see if they have any further questions to put to the witness in the light of the questions put by the Trial Chamber. Do you have any other questions for this witness? Mr. Withopf, or Mrs. Benjamin?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Witness, this concludes your examination. You have answered the questions put to you both by the Prosecution and by the Defence, as well as to the questions put to you by the Trial Chamber. Thank you for your testimony. We wish you a good trip home. The usher will now escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you once more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the Prosecution if the witness scheduled for today is present.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the witness is present. However, there's an issue I would like to discuss in private session, prior to the witness being called in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll ask the registrar now to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness. Are you receiving the interpretation of what I am saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you've been called here as a witness for the Prosecution in a case that the Trial Chamber is responsible for. In order to testify before this Court, you must first tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Mijo Marijanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born on the 29th of September in Kupres, in the village of Ocinovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What is your current status? Are you retired? Are you still working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't retired yet. I'm not receiving any pension benefits at the moment. I am being cared for by the Red Cross and social welfare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can you tell us, in 1993, ten years ago, what was your profession? What sort of position did you hold at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, I worked as a driver in the Bugojno medical centre. And I was an official for procurement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As you will be testifying before this Trial Chamber, you have to make a solemn declaration. The usher who is by your side will show you a text, and I would be grateful if you could read it out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do I have to stand up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Given your condition, you can remain sitting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You have just made a solemn declaration before testifying. Before we proceed, could you tell us whether you have already testified in court or is this the first time for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Representatives of the Prosecution have informed us that you have certain medical problems at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we will have a break every 40 or 45 minutes in order to allow you to rest. If in the course of the examination you would like a break, do tell us. We will adjourn the hearing at your request. So if you feel it is necessary to have the hearing adjourned, let us know and we will adjourn it. First of all, I would like to inform you of the procedure to be followed. You're going to now have to answer questions that will be put to you by representatives of the Prosecution. The Prosecution is to your right. In a short while, a representative of the Prosecution will be asking you some questions. Insofar as it is possible, try to provide us with complete answers to the extent that you can remember the events that took place over ten years ago. If you're unable to answer a question, if you have forgotten something , if you are incapable of answering a question, be frank and tell us. If the question put to you seems too difficult or if you don't understand it, ask the person putting the question to you to rephrase the question. When the Prosecution has concluded its examination, the Defence, who are to your left - there are five of them, but only two of them will be asking you questions - if they feel it is necessary, the Defence will cross-examine you. The questions that they will put to you will have to do with the questions put to you by the Prosecution or will have to do with the context at the time, because the Defence also has to verify certain facts that you will be testifying about. The objective of these questions is to make matters clear for the Judges, who are before. If the Judges feel that it is necessary, they may also ask you questions in order to clarify matters that may have arisen in the course of the examination of the cross-examination. If you feel that there are difficulties of any kind, let us know and we will adjourn the hearing. It is now quarter past 3.00. We will proceed for about 40 minutes and we will adjourn at ten to 4.00. Have you understood everything I have said? Witness, have you understood what I have just told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Prosecution, Mr. Withopf, you have the floor. You may begin your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Marijanovic.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon to you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Marijanovic, can you please tell the Trial Chamber where, in which town you grew up.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: In Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please also inform the Trial Chamber where you lived in spring and summer of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Also in Bugojno, and I was detained as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: We will come to your detention later on, Mr. Marijanovic. Have you ever been a member of the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA. When did you do your military service for the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, that. That was in 1966. And I completed in 1967.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You already mentioned a few minutes ago that you were arrested in 1993. Do you still recall as to when you were arrested? Do you know -- do you still recall the month in which you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was in July, between the 18th and the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Between the 18th and the 23rd of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please tell us who arrested you.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Once you were arrested by the BiH army in July 1993, where were you brought to?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was brought to the basement of the grammar school. This is the place where coal and fuel wood used to be kept for the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You just said you were arrested by the army, by the ABiH. Were you arrested by soldiers of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were all soldiers. They all wore uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the soldiers who arrested you, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. They had all sorts of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please briefly describe the sort of weapons, all sort of weapons they had.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I could tell, they had Kalashnikovs, they had some machine-guns, and automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: At the time you were arrested, Mr. Marijanovic, were you a civilian or were you a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, I was a member of the HVO. At that time, I was on a leave, on a week's leave, and I wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: After you were arrested and brought to the school, what did happen to you?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: They arrested me, my wife, and my daughter. They took us to the basement, where there were three cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform us about the size of the cells in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately 3 by 3 or 3 by 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To your recollection, Mr. Marijanovic, were all these cells, all the three cells, of the same or similar size?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: They were almost identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Once you were brought to this cell in the basement, were there already any other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you inform the Trial Chamber how many other prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: In every cell there were approximately 35 to 40 people. I was taken to just one cell, and that is the only cell I could see. I couldn't see what was happening in other two cells. It was dark, and you know what basements usually look like. They're dark; they don't have any windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Just as a matter for clarification, Mr. Marijanovic, how many people, how many detainees were imprisoned in the cell you were detained?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Between 35 and 40. It was dark. It was night. I couldn't count them. But the cell was crowded. You couldn't even sit down. You had to remain standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, can you please inform us about the ethnic background of the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: They were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The detainees, Mr. Marijanovic, you are --

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Most of them were Croats. Almost 99 per cent of them were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the detained Croats, were they civilians or were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: There were both civilians and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were just mentioning, Mr. Marijanovic, that together with you, your wife and your daughter were arrested. Were they also brought to the basement of the school?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course. However, they separated us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the age of your daughter at the time.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Nineteen, twenty.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were arrested in July 1993. Would you please tell us about the temperature in the cell you were detained.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was deadly. We didn't have a thermometer, but we were all sweating profusely. We could hardly breathe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform, Mr. Marijanovic, can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the sanitary conditions in the cell.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: There were none. We didn't have water. We didn't have a toilet. They had to take us outside, or they would bring us a bottle of water. It all depended on their whim.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please also inform us about the food you were given in the cell.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: There was none in the grammar school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Mr. Marijanovic, whilst you were detained in the grammar school that you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: On a couple of occasions, they took me out to some other room and they beat me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please provide us with some more detail about the beatings.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a room there. It was not a classroom. Most probably it was the teachers' room, where the teachers used to have their meals. This was the room where they beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the ones who beat you, did they use any tools to beat you?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: They used all sorts of things. They used sticks, fists, rubber batons; whatever they had they used.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please also tell us on what parts of your body you were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was facing them, so they slapped me. They hit me on the chest, in the stomach. If I wasn't facing them, then they hit me in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You're telling us about the beatings you got. Were the other detainees also beaten?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Everybody was beaten. Everybody fared the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And for how long, Mr. Marijanovic, did these beatings last? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes it took less, sometimes it took more, depending on the person who did the beating. I didn't have a wristwatch, so I -- I didn't know the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And do you still recall, Mr. Marijanovic, whether the ones who beat you were civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: They were all soldiers, to the last. They all wore uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And do you know, Mr. Marijanovic, to which army they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: They told us every time that they were BiH army soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Whilst you were detained in the basement, were you guarded there?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. In the vicinity, they were so close that they could overhear our conversations. We were afraid to talk to each other because we were afraid they would take us out for beating if they heard us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the ones who guarded you there, were they also soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. They all wore uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And were they also soldiers of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: They told me that they were all BiH army soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, after the break I will show the witness two photographs in relation to the school building. Unfortunately, the Sanction technology is not working at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have those photos?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: We do have the photos, the hard copies available. However, the Sanction technology is not working. The one has actually already been tendered in the past, and there would be a second one, which would be a new one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Maybe your screen is out of order and the others may be working. I don't know. Can you check? If not, maybe you can provide us with the hard copy of your photos and you can ask questions based on the hard copy of the photographs that you're going to show to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, the first photograph I intended to show the witness is a photograph which has already been tendered into evidence. For the purpose of identification, I wanted to use the Sanction technology only. The second one, however, is a new one and the hard copy is available now. Can the witness please be shown the paragraph ERN 01248102.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it has been admitted under what number, please? The exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: This one -- I apologise. This one, Mr. President, hasn't been admitted yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. So this is a new exhibit, a new photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to show the photo to the witness, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Marijanovic, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, can you please tell us what you can see on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can see the cells in the grammar school which have been redecorated in the meantime and turned into a workshop. The cells have been tidied up. But I recognise the windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you recognise the room on this photograph as the cell you were detained?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am 100 per cent sure that this is the cell. I recognise the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Marijanovic, can you please date and sign the photograph. Today is the 12th of February, 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, can you put your name on the photo and today's date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please show the photo to the Prosecution, to the Defence, to the accused. The Chamber makes note of the name, of the date. Can we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit P64.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P64. We have five minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For how long, Mr. Marijanovic, were you detained in this cell of the school?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly. Maybe 10, 15, or even 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what happened afterwards? Were you released or were you brought to where else -- somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: They took us to another basement, this time to the basement of a furniture store.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And in saying "they took us to another basement," namely the basement of the furniture store, whom are you referring to when you say "they"?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: They came in a van that looked like a refrigerator lorry, and they put us in. We were like pigs in that van. They drove us around the town. And then they unloaded us. I said, "Why did it take you so long to bring us to a place which is only two minutes away?" My conclusion was that they wanted to somehow mask where they were taking us. They didn't want us to know where we were being taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And this furniture salon you were brought to, how far away is it actually from the school you were detained first?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. 100 or maybe 150 metres approximately. I never measured the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Once you arrived, Mr. Marijanovic, once you arrived at the furniture salon, what did happen to you?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: They put us in the basement. The basement was flooded. There were no seats. There was nowhere for us to sit or -- we had to stand in the water. The situation was desperate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were all detainees from the school brought to the Slavonija Furniture Salon?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And for clarification, what did happen to your wife and your daughter, who were also detained in the school?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: They were transferred to the Vojin Paleksic School.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were just about, Mr. Marijanovic, just about to describe the room you were detained in the furniture -- Slavonija Furniture Salon. What was the size, roughly, of this room?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe about half the size of this room, but the conditions were terrible. The room was flooded. Not even mice could live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What does it actually mean, "the room was flooded"? Can you please provide us with some more detail.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Water was up to our ankles or even higher. There was some 10 centimetres of water on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And do you recall how many prisoners were detained in this basement of the Slavonija Furniture Salon?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the grammar school cells, there were 35 to 40 people in every cell, so you can do the maths. And some other people were taken as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Does this mean that in the Slavonija Furniture Salon, in the basement of the Slavonija Furniture Salon there were not only detainees from the grammar school?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, there were others too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the ethnic background of the people detained in the Slavonija Furniture Salon.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Most of them were Croats. As far as I know, there was only one Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think it would be best to have a break now. It is ten to 4.00. We'll have a half-an-hour break and we'll resume at twenty past 4.00. Witness, during this half-an-hour break, the usher will enable you to get some fresh air and we will resume in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now resume. There's been a change in the Defence team. The Trial Chamber would like to greet Mr. Bourgon, who has just arrived. Can we proceed, or would you like to wait for Mrs. Residovic to arrive?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'll take the place of Mrs. Residovic for a short while, but she will be joining us soon, so we may continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We may proceed. Please go ahead, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Marijanovic, you were just informing the Trial Chamber that in the basement of the Slavonija Furniture Salon the detainees were all Croats and one Serb detainee. The detainees, were they soldiers or were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: There were some civilians, but most of them were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I'm going to show you now, Mr. Marijanovic, a further photograph. It will appear on the screen in front of you and you will also be given a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the hard copies are available for distribution. And for the information of the Trial Chamber and Defence, this photograph was taken in the course of 2002 in the course of the investigation against the two accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Marijanovic, can you please tell the Trial Chamber what you can see on this photograph in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the building of the furniture salon, of the furniture shop. But in the basement they had storage space, and the shop was upstairs, and there were some offices upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Is this the building in whose basement you were detained?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Marijanovic, can you please date - today is the 12th of February, 2004 - and sign the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber would like to ask the witness a question. Can you leave the photograph there before the witness. Witness, you said that the furniture shop was in that building. In 1993, when you were taken to that building, what we can see to the right, it seems to be a car park, a three-storey car park. Did that exist at the time? So the building to the right in the photograph, did it exist at the time, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, it didn't exist then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And to the left, we can see a large building that consists of a number of floors. There are -- it's a block of flats. And we can see some satellites. At the time, did this building exist, this building with the satellite dishes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when you were taken to the building, the person -- the persons who lived in the building to the left may have seen you arrive; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, some did and some didn't. I don't know exactly who saw that event and how much they saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Withopf, do you want to tender this document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Yes, I wish to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have an exhibit number, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be P65.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P65.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Marijanovic, I'm now going to show you another photograph. It will appear on the screen in front of you and you will again be given a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Again, this photograph was taken in 2002 in the course of the investigation against the accused Hadzihasanovic and Kubura.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll never forget this building. That is the basement in Slavonija ^Slavonjalis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You already started to tell us what you can see on the photograph. Is this the basement of the Slavonija Furniture Salon you were detained?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And you can see that there was water in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What you can see on this photograph, Mr. Marijanovic - the photograph was taken years later in 2002 - however, does this photograph -- is the situation in respect to the water on the floor similar to the situation you faced during your detention in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it was no worse, but no better either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Marijanovic, can you please again, please sign the photograph and date it.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, could we have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be P66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P66. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Marijanovic, for how long have you been detained in this basement of the Slavonija Furniture Salon?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, 15 or 20 days, but I don't know how long exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And for the duration of your detention in the basement of the Slavonija Furniture Salon, was there any light in the basement?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: There wasn't any light, but the nuns would give us some oil and some of the men had bandages which we used as filters. So this provided us with a little light and enabled us to avoid treading in the water where it was a little deeper.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the sanitary conditions in this basement whilst you were detained.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the sanitary conditions -- you can see the water. We would go up. They would only allow us to go to the toilet and get some water there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the food you were provided with, if any.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we didn't get any food there. All we got is what the civilians would bring us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Are you aware of any beatings whilst you were detained in the basement of the Slavonija Furniture Salon?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. They'd put paper bags over their heads so that we couldn't recognise them. Young Havro died. He died as a result of the beating. Havranek died.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did the beatings take place in the basement, in the detention cell, or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Up in the shop. There was a sort of warehouse downstairs. They'd take people up to the shop, and they had various implements up there. They'd have those paper bags, various things. They'd use whatever they could get their hands on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please provide us with some more detail what they actually used for the beatings.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: There were wooden implements, rods -- iron rods, truncheons, police truncheons, various sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And how did you get to know about these implements which were used for the beatings?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a toilet upstairs, and when we passed by it, we would see these weapons, the truncheons and the bags that they used.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And how often -- how often were the beatings inflicted on the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number. It depended on the shift, and sometimes it would just occur to someone. One person would call another one to join in. People were afraid that they would be beaten, that they would call out to the others to beat them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: A few minutes ago, you said, Mr. Marijanovic, that one of the detainees - namely, Havranek, died as a result of the beating. Can you please provide the Trial Chamber with more details about the death of Mr. Havranek.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they called him. We heard him groaning, shouting. He said, "Stop." He told them to stop beating him. He was not able to move. They called the men from the basement to take him to the clinic. And after five or six steps -- well, I went with these young men to see who would be carrying him. And I saw when five or six of them got hold of Havranek, I saw that he seemed to be bleeding inside. The clinic isn't far, but he died in their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You are making reference to the fact that "they called him." Whom are you actually referring to? Who are "they"?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, those guards, the troops, whatever they called them. The people who guarded us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You are saying the troops? Just for clarification, the one who is guarded you, were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: They were all in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, which army did they form part of?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: The BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were the soldiers of the BiH army who guarded you the ones who beat you as well?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they had shifts which would change. So sometimes you wouldn't be able to recognise them since they'd put paper bags on your head.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: How did you get to know, Mr. Marijanovic, that the detainee with the name Havranek died in their hands whilst taken to the clinic?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I found out about that immediately, when I saw that he had internal bleeding and that his stomach was swelling. And after they'd taken five or six steps in the direction of the clinic, he died. When the young men returned, they would say that young Havranek had died.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the young men who tried to bring Mr. Havranek to the clinic, were they also detained together with you in the furniture salon?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Havranek, whose son was Mr. Havranek, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: He was the son of Stasko Havranek.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Whilst you were detained in the furniture salon, Mr. Marijanovic, did there come a time when you were taken out for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know who this person was, perhaps a lawyer. He didn't introduce himself. He asked me whether I'd fired any shots. I said, "Please have a look at my weapon and you'll see for yourself that it hasn't been used."

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And do you still recall where you were taken to for the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a sports building where they'd play handball, basketball. That's where they took us. It was in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And after the interrogation, were you brought back to the Slavonija Furniture Salon?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You told us that you were detained in the Slavonija Furniture Salon for a number of days. Did there come a time when you were transferred to somewhere else? And if so, can you please tell us where to.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Occasionally they would call me to clean the area around the building, and then we were transferred to the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Does this stadium have a name?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was Iskra Stadium. The name of the football club was Iskra at the time, so we called it the Iskra Stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And in which town is this Iskra Stadium located?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't far. Behind a stream -- over a stream, where you could build such a building. There was sufficient space there. But it was closer to the town than is usually the case when stadiums are built.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The town you are referring to, is it Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit P62. We will only use the Sanction technology.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Marijanovic, in front of you on the screen you do see a building. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber what you can see.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the Iskra Stadium. And I will remember this building for as long as I live. This part of the building was built so that they could detain us there. You see that this part of the building is under the stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For the record, the witness identifies the building in Prosecution Exhibit P62 as the FC Iskra Stadium building in which he was detained. Mr. Marijanovic, once you were transferred to the FC Iskra Stadium what did happen to you?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: We stayed there for a while. After some time, 50 of us were transferred to Gornji Vakuf to dig trenches there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Let's go step by step, Mr. Marijanovic. You stayed there for a while. Did you actually stay in a cell?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a common room. What you see on the very left is something that was added on subsequently. Those were not cells. They were somewhat larger rooms, larger than a normal cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And how many people were detained together with you in this larger room?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: There were about 300 people there once they were all brought in. There were 300 people altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And were the 300 people altogether all detained in the very same larger room?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We all shared that one large room, until the moment the smaller room was added to the complex at the far-left end.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform us about the ethnic background of the detainees in the FC Iskra Stadium.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I've already told you. The majority, maybe 99 per cent, were Croats. There was just one Serb, if I can remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And again, the question - and it relates to the FC Iskra Stadium, Mr. Marjanovic - the detainees, were they soldiers or civilians, or a mixture of both?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: There were all sorts of people. There were elderly people. Some of them were even older than -- than I am now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And were there also soldiers amongst them, amongst the detainees?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the elderly people, the ones you are identifying as being -- having been older than you are now, were they soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: They were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Who guarded the FC Iskra Stadium whilst you were detained there?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, all the guards wore uniform. Their commander was somebody called Kukavica. I don't know whether this was his nickname or his family name. The guards worked in shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And do you know, Mr. Marijanovic, which army the guards in uniforms formed part of?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: They would always tell me that they belonged to the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Whilst you were detained in the FC Iskra Stadium, did you become aware of any beatings inflicted on the detainees?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. People would be taken to the bank. A few people were beaten. I was also beaten, together with another person called Zeljo. We were beaten on the stands. His glasses were broken. And the others were taken to the Beobanka building, to the basement of that building. When they came back, we could see them walking very slowly and with a lot of difficulty. And we could also see bruises on their bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please provide the Trial Chamber with some more details about the beatings inflicted on you.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: On one occasion, I was taken out to the stands together with Zeljo from Gornji Vakuf. On another occasion, as I was on my way to the toilet, we were forced to run the gauntlet and we were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were other detainees beaten as well?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: We were all beaten in a similar way. Some were beaten more heavily; some were beaten less heavily. I don't know whether everybody was beaten, but most of us were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the ones who beat you, were they the same ones as guarding the FC Iskra Stadium?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Almost the same people. They didn't use batons or sticks because they were afraid that people who came to visit us would see tools in their hands. That's why we would be taken to the stands, so that people who were watching from the direction of Bugojno could not see how we were being beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Marijanovic, I'm now going to show you a further photograph. And it will appear on the screen in front of you and you will also be given a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the Iskra Stadium, with the stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You already answered my question, Mr. Marijanovic. Are these the stands where you and the others were beaten?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: A hundred per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Again, this photograph has been taken in 2002 in the course of the investigation against the two accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Marijanovic, again, can you please sign the photograph and date it.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The Prosecution wishes to tender this photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, thank you very much. Mr. Registrar, can we have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number P67.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Marijanovic, for how long were you detained in the FC Iskra Stadium in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Altogether, eight months. And if you deduct the time that I spent in Gornji Vakuf, where I was for 30 to 50 days, then you can do the maths and come to the figure, the number of days that I spent at the stadium. I was detained for eight months altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please provide, Mr. Marijanovic, some detail about the sanitary conditions in the FC Iskra Stadium.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: There was just one toilet, which was clogged. So we had to use makeshift toilets. We only had one hose for water, and at their whim they would turn the tap on to allow us to fill bottles with water. But that was at their own whim. There was no soap. There was nothing to use to wash ourselves with. There was nothing. No hygiene could be practiced.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please also inform us about the food conditions whilst you were detained in the FC Iskra Stadium.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: At first we didn't have anything. And later on they would bring us lentils or something. The food I had never heard of or seen. It's something that you wouldn't even give to pigs. And then civilians started bringing us food when they allowed them to do that. If they hadn't done that and if civilians hadn't brought us food, I don't know what would have happened to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please also tell us how and where you slept.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: At first we slept on the concrete floor, on the bare concrete floor. And later on, the guys who were sent out to work brought some wooden boards back and we used that to sleep on. And then the International Community brought us a blanket each, and we used that for bedding. And this was a big improvement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you recall for how long you had to sleep on the concrete floor?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: It must have been for more than 20 or even 30 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were mentioning earlier on, Mr. Marijanovic, that you were taken out to Gornji Vakuf. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber who took you out to Gornji Vakuf and what you actually did in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: The army from Gornji Vakuf came with a lorry, and they took 50 of us up there. And then they assigned us to various tasks. We had to dig trenches, canals. We had to erect brick walls for protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The army from Gornji Vakuf, are you referring to the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm referring to the BH army. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were just saying, Mr. Marijanovic, that you had to dig -- amongst other things, that you had to dig trenches. Can you please provide us with some more detail about the trench-digging.

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: I and two other men were forced to dig trenches on the so-called Relej. It's a hill, a very steep hill. I was forced to do that for a few days. But then they could see that I couldn't move easily. The slope was very steep. I was transferred then to do something else, and the other two continued digging the trench on that hill slope.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And who did force you to dig trenches and the others?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: The BH army. They were all in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And whilst you were forced digging trenches by the ABiH, did there come a time when you were exposed to some fire?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Not me personally, but another man was killed and two other men were injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The trenches you and the others were forced to dig by ABiH army soldiers, were they close to any HVO positions?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, the distance was about 200 metres or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And how did it happen that a man, to your knowledge, was killed and two other men were injured whilst digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: The two were wounded on this hill. One was wounded in the hip, and the other in the butt. Anto Barisic was wounded in the hip, and Dominik Bozo was wounded in his butt. Zeljo was killed. I believe that he was killed from a sniper. And they said that it was our guys who did that. The distance was so big that I believe that he was shot from a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Anto Barisic and Dominik Bozo --

utterances.speaker: MIJO MARIJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were wounded. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know what the objective of these questions is; however, for five or six minutes the Prosecution has been asking questions which are not relevant to the indictment. Secondly, the area of Gornji Vakuf was not the area under the control of the 3rd Corps, so I don't see the point of the questions that fall within this scope. I don't know why this witness is being asked these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Withopf, I believe that your questions refer to the fact that the prisoners were taken out to the front line to dig trenches. The other things that you've mentioned do not form part of the indictment and are not relevant to the indictment. Have you taken note of the observations made by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I certainly have taken note of the observations made by the Defence. I, however, wish to draw the attention of both the Trial Chamber and Defence to the respective portions of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, in which the relevance of these events is detailed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's on page 104 and 105, where you indicate that "Prisoners were taken to dig trenches on the front line" and that "they didn't receive food at regular intervals." But you don't mention that they were exposed to sniper fire and that one of them was killed. This is not in the indictment. However, he said it spontaneously, without being prompted. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would, however, ask for the Prosecution not to be allowed to continue asking questions about prisoners being taken to do work for another reason. The Prosecution did have such counts in the indictment; however, objections were raised to the indictment and the Trial Chamber ordered for the indictment to be amended and in the Second Amended Indictment the Prosecutor withdrew those counts. The Third Indictment does not contain these counts either. And since the Prosecutor asked the same questions of the previous witness and continues with this witness again, I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to order the Prosecution not to pursue this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. I believe that he should not pursue this line of questioning. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Again, I refer to the respective portions of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, in which the relevance of this line of questioning is detailed. Unfortunately, I don't have the pre-trial brief in front of me, therefore I can't make reference to the specific paragraphs. However, it's the view of the Prosecution that these issues pertain to Count 4, Cruel Treatment, of the Third Amended Indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the documents in English, on page 58, it says that "The prisoners were taken to dig trenches. They did forced labour on the front line." That's in paragraph 125.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Completely correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: It's correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I am just about to check it on the electronic version, and you are making reference to the exact right paragraph. It's paragraph 125 of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has been indicated that the prisoners did do forced labour, and the rest is just marginal. He told us that he had been taken to a certain place to do work. What he didn't say in his response was who the enemies were. Were they Serbs? Were they Croats? Who were the trenches being dug against? Who was on the other side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they were Croats. This clarifies things for me. So Croats were shooting at you while you were working.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They wouldn't have shot at me. I could walk around freely. And there were a few of us who were in the group, and they would not shoot at us. If they had been shooting, they would have wounded me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
